\chapter{Not}
\label{ch:it-non}
\hlchaptermodality{30}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can turn any sentence in this book over with non, say that I do not understand, use né … né and neanche, and say that something is or is not there.}

The chapter's last lesson takes non c'è male apart, twenty-eight chapters after Chapter 2 handed it over whole and said its negation and its c'è would come back on their own ramps. Both have.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[non]{non — the word that turns a sentence over}

\label{lesson:IT-C30-non}



\begin{quote}
A new chapter, and the word it opens with has been quietly present since the wellbeing chapter.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{vero?} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sì} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ottenere} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{rispondere} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{parlare} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the rule, in one line}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{non} goes \textbf{immediately before the verb}. That is the whole rule.
\end{quote}

Everything you have been taught to say can now be said the other way round:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{you had} & \textbf{you now also have} \\
\midrule
\emph{Parlo italiano.} & \emph{\textbf{Non} parlo italiano.} — I don't speak Italian. \\
\emph{Prendo il caffè.} & \emph{\textbf{Non} prendo il caffè.} — I'm not having the coffee. \\
\emph{Abito a Roma.} & \emph{\textbf{Non} abito a Roma.} \\
\emph{Ho venti anni.} & \emph{\textbf{Non} ho venti anni.} \\
\emph{Sono d'accordo.} & \emph{\textbf{Non} sono d'accordo.} — I don't agree. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That last one matters. Until this line, this book could agree — \emph{d'accordo}, one lesson ago — and could not disagree with anything at all.

Italian does \textbf{not} need a helper verb the way English does. English has to borrow \emph{do} (\emph{I speak} $\to$ \emph{I \textbf{do} not speak}). Italian puts one small word in front of the verb it already had, and stops.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Non} is Latin \textbf{nōn} — the same Latin word as the \emph{no} of the last lesson but one. Stressed, it became \textbf{no} and learned to stand alone. Unstressed, it became \textbf{non} and learned to lean on a verb. Neither can do the other's job.

The \emph{non c'è male} lesson gave it to you as a single frozen lump and said, in as many words, that its negation and its \emph{c'è} would come back later on their own ramps. This is the first half of that promise. The second half is four lessons away.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{non}
  \item \emph{Non parlo italiano.}
  \item \emph{Non prendo il caffè.}
  \item \emph{Non sono d'accordo.}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \emph{non} go? (\textbf{Immediately before the verb}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I don't agree.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Non sono d'accordo}}.) Which Latin word is behind both \emph{no} and \emph{non}? (\emph{\textbf{Nōn}} — one word split by stress.) And which frozen phrase from the wellbeing chapter has been carrying \emph{non} all along? (\emph{\textbf{Non c'è male}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[non capisco]{non capisco — saying you have not followed}

\label{lesson:IT-C30-non-capisco}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back, one chapter back, and two long throws.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{non} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{no} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{il caffè} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{il tè} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{abitare} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the two things to say when you are lost}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Capisco.} — I understand. \textbf{Non capisco.} — I don't understand.
\end{quote}

Both halves were already in the building. The \emph{capire} lesson taught the verb and gave \textbf{capisco} first in its paradigm. The last lesson gave you \textbf{non}. Nothing new is being learnt here except the fact that you may now put them together — and that this is the single most useful sentence a beginner owns.

The \emph{prego?} lesson taught you the rising \textbf{Prego?} that asks somebody to say it again. Use the two in order:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Non capisco. Prego?} — I don't understand. Say it again?
\end{quote}

\emph{Prego?} asks for a repeat. \emph{Non capisco} tells the other person that repeating it the same way will not help, so they will slow down or choose different words. An Italian speaker who hears only \emph{Prego?} will simply say the same sentence again, at the same speed.

A slower and gentler version, for when you have caught some of it:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Non capisco bene.} — I don't quite understand.
\end{quote}

\emph{Bene} is the wellbeing chapter's, doing new work.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Capisco.}
  \item \emph{Non capisco.}
  \item \emph{Non capisco. Prego?}
  \item \emph{Non capisco bene.}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I don't understand.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textbf{Non capisco}}.) Which chapter gave you \emph{capisco}? (\textbf{The} \emph{\textbf{capire}} \textbf{lesson}.) Why say \emph{non capisco} rather than only \emph{prego?} (\emph{\textbf{Prego?}} \textbf{asks for a repeat; \emph{non capisco} asks for a different sentence.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[né … né]{né … né — neither one nor the other}

\label{lesson:IT-C30-ne}



\begin{quote}
Three lessons of this chapter behind you already.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{non capisco} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sì, grazie / no, grazie} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{il latte} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{lo zucchero} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{lavorare} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the pair, and the doubled negative}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{né … né} — \textbf{neither … nor}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Non prendo né caffè né tè.} — I'll have neither coffee nor tea. \textbf{Non ho né fratelli né sorelle.} — I have neither brothers nor sisters.
\end{quote}

Read that first Italian sentence again and count the negatives. There are \textbf{three}: \emph{non}, and \emph{né}, and \emph{né}. English allows only one and calls a second one an error. Italian requires them all, and a sentence with \emph{né} and no \emph{non} is simply wrong:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Wrong:} \emph{Prendo né caffè né tè.} \textbf{Right:} \textbf{Non} prendo \textbf{né} caffè \textbf{né} tè.
\end{quote}

This is why \emph{né} comes after \emph{non} in this book rather than before it. Without \emph{non} there is nothing for it to stand beside.

The accent is doing the same job it did on \emph{sì}: it separates \textbf{né} from \textbf{ne}, a different unstressed word.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{né … né}
  \item \emph{Non prendo né caffè né tè.}
  \item \emph{Non ho né fratelli né sorelle.}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Italian say \textquotedblleft{}neither … nor\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Né … né}}.) How many negatives does \emph{Non prendo né caffè né tè} contain? (\textbf{Three} — and Italian wants all three.) What happens if you drop the \emph{non}? (\textbf{The sentence is wrong} — \emph{né} cannot stand without it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[anche / neanche]{anche — me too, and me neither}

\label{lesson:IT-C30-anche}



\begin{quote}
The fourth word of the chapter, and the one that finally explains a line you heard among the first \emph{-are} verbs.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{né … né} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{d'accordo} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{l'amico, l'amica} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{la famiglia} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{Parlo italiano} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{anche} — \textbf{also, too, as well}.
\end{quote}

It goes in front of whatever it adds:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Prendo il caffè. Prendo anche il latte.} — I'm having coffee. I'm also having milk. \textbf{Anche Marco abita a Roma.} — Marco lives in Rome too.
\end{quote}

And on its own, agreeing with somebody:

\begin{quote}
— \textbf{Parlo un po' d'italiano.} — \textbf{Anch'io.} — Me too.
\end{quote}

You have heard \textbf{anch'io} already. It is in the \emph{parlo un po'} dialogue, said once and never explained, because that chapter was busy with verb endings. It is \emph{anche} + \emph{io}, with the vowel elided — the same elision as \emph{l'acqua} and \emph{d'accordo}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{neanche} — \textbf{neither, not … either, not even}.
\end{quote}

It is \textbf{né} + \textbf{anche}, welded into one word, and you were given the first half one lesson ago. Because it carries a \emph{né}, it keeps the \emph{non} rule with it:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Non prendo neanche il tè.} — I'm not having tea either.
\end{quote}

Standing alone, answering somebody, the \emph{non} has nowhere to sit and drops away:

\begin{quote}
— \textbf{Non capisco.} — \textbf{Neanch'io.} — Me neither.
\end{quote}

So the pair to learn is \textbf{anch'io / neanch'io} — \emph{me too} and \emph{me neither} — which between them answer most of what anybody says to you.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{anche}
  \item \emph{Anch'io.}
  \item \emph{neanche}
  \item \emph{Neanch'io.}
  \item \emph{Non prendo neanche il tè.}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{anche} mean? (\textbf{Also, too}.) Which two words is \emph{neanche} made of? (\emph{\textbf{Né}} \textbf{+} \emph{\textbf{anche}}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}me too\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}me neither\textquotedblright{}. (\emph{\textbf{Anch'io}} — \emph{\textbf{neanch'io}}.) Where in this book had you already heard \emph{anch'io}? (\textbf{In the} \emph{\textbf{parlo un po'}} \textbf{dialogue}, where it was never glossed.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[c'è / ci sono]{c'è, ci sono — there is, there are}

\label{lesson:IT-C30-ce}



\begin{quote}
The chapter closes by taking apart a phrase you were given twenty-eight chapters ago.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{anche / neanche} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back, before it decays
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{vero?} — \textbf{R2}, the first real retrieval, five to fifteen lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{il nome} — \textbf{R3}, durable, twenty to sixty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{la persona} — \textbf{R3}, durable again, a second word from that distance
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{(practice)} — \textbf{R4}, recognition at distance, eighty lessons back or more
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the two forms}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{c'è} — \textbf{there is} (one thing) \textbf{ci sono} — \textbf{there are} (more than one)
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{C'è un caffè.} — There is a coffee. \textbf{Ci sono due amici.} — There are two friends.
\end{quote}

The verb is \emph{essere}, which its own lesson gave you: \textbf{è} is its third person singular and \textbf{sono} its third person plural. All that is new is the little \textbf{ci} in front, and the apostrophe when \emph{ci} meets \emph{è}.

Italian chooses between them by counting what follows, exactly as English does with \emph{is} and \emph{are}. What Italian does \textbf{not} do is what English does with \emph{there}: English uses the same word for the place (\emph{over there}) and for the construction (\emph{there is}). Italian keeps them apart — the place words are the next chapter's.

\begin{cousinweb}
The wellbeing chapter taught you \textbf{non c'è male} as a single unbroken lump, and its lesson said outright that the negation and the \emph{c'è} inside it belonged to later lessons. Both have now arrived, so the lump comes apart:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{non} — not \emph{(four lessons ago)} \textbf{c'è} — there is \emph{(this lesson)} \textbf{male} — badly, ill \emph{(the wellbeing chapter)}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Non c'è male} is, word for word, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{there isn't any bad}.\textquotedblright{} It is not a special idiom for \textquotedblleft{}not bad\textquotedblright{}; it is an ordinary Italian sentence that you were handed early because you needed an answer before you could build one. You can now build it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{c'è}
  \item \emph{ci sono}
  \item \emph{C'è un caffè.}
  \item \emph{Ci sono due amici.}
  \item \emph{Non c'è male.}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}there is\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{C'è}}.) And \textquotedblleft{}there are\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Ci sono}}.) Take \emph{non c'è male} apart. (\emph{\textbf{Non}} \textbf{+} \emph{\textbf{c'è}} \textbf{+} \emph{\textbf{male}} — \textquotedblleft{}there isn't any bad\textquotedblright{}.) Which lesson promised you this? (\textbf{The} \emph{\textbf{non c'è male}} \textbf{lesson}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
